title: Relational Algebra Expressions
description: Compose selections, projections and joins from a precise result contract, trace intermediate relation shapes, and distinguish safe logical rewrites from physical execution.
notes:
## An expression composes operations into a result

A relational algebra expression describes a result by applying operators to input relations. Each operator produces another relation that can become an input to a later operator. This closure property lets a complicated question be built from understandable steps. The purpose is to state the requested facts precisely, rather than prescribing the exact machine instructions a database must execute.

Consider students(student_id, name, department, gpa). The question asks for names of Engineering students whose GPA is at least 3.5. Selection first identifies qualifying student tuples. Projection then keeps name. In classical set algebra, projection removes duplicate resulting tuples. Ordinary SQL SELECT does not automatically remove repeated names, so translating the expression requires deciding whether the output represents people or distinct name values.

## Begin with the output grain and population

Write what one result row means before choosing operators. One row per qualifying student needs student_id if different students can share a name. One row per distinct displayed name intentionally collapses those different identities. The English word names can hide that difference, so make the contract explicit instead of treating DISTINCT as a harmless formatting preference.

Next identify the candidate population. An Engineering student report starts from students, whereas a report of enrollment occurrences can start from enrollments and attach student properties. These choices affect students without enrollments, repeated occurrences, and the keys carried through intermediate results. A recognizable final column label does not compensate for choosing the wrong initial population.

## Read nested notation from its inputs outward

An expression such as project name of select department equals Engineering from students is evaluated logically from the base students relation outward. The selection's input is students; its output still has the student attributes. The projection's input is that selected relation, and its output has only name. Parentheses show composition in the same way nested function calls do.

For a conjunction of department and GPA predicates, both properties must be available where the selection applies. Projecting only name before testing GPA loses a required attribute. Projection can move earlier only when it retains everything later operations need, including join attributes, predicate attributes, and final output attributes. Reason about available roles, not merely about whether a shorter expression looks tidy.

## Trace intermediate headings and membership

Suppose Student 1 is Asha in Engineering with GPA 3.8, Student 2 is Asha in Engineering with GPA 3.6, and Student 3 is Ben in Science with GPA 3.9. Selecting Engineering and GPA at least 3.5 leaves the two Asha identities. Projecting only name under set semantics leaves one Asha value. A student-grain report still has two rows.

A useful trace records each intermediate heading, the identity represented, and the membership rule. This makes mistakes visible before optimizing anything. If an intermediate result no longer contains department_id, it cannot later match Departments by that role. If an operator changes the grain from students to enrollment occurrences, later counts need to reflect that changed population.

## Joins introduce relationships and multiplicity

To report department names with qualifying students, combine students.department_id with departments.department_id using the intended identity predicate. The join attaches a matching department fact. It does not independently authorize access, create a foreign key, or guarantee every student has a corresponding department. Those properties require their own source constraints and application boundaries.

Adding enrollments changes multiplicity. One student with three qualifying enrollments can appear three times in an ordinary inner join result. If the output asks only which students have at least one qualifying enrollment, an existence predicate can express that membership directly. Adding DISTINCT afterward may yield the desired set, but first understand why the join generated repeated student rows.

## Three inputs need explicit association roles

A report of Engineering students enrolled in open courses can combine students, enrollments and courses. The first association connects enrollments.student_id to students.student_id. The second connects enrollments.course_id to courses.course_id. Filtering students.department and courses.is_open then restricts the intended rows. Selecting the final columns determines whether the report shows participation occurrences or distinct students.

A shared column name is not enough evidence for a valid association. Several tables may expose status with unrelated meanings, and course identifiers may have program-local scope. Name each actual relationship and include its complete key. Aliases distinguish roles, especially when the same relation is used twice for relationships such as student and mentor.

## Translate the intended set to SQL deliberately

The first exercise requests distinct name values rather than distinct student identities. Its SQL therefore includes DISTINCT after the selection. This is a deliberate bridge from classical projection semantics to SQL's default duplicate-preserving result behaviour. Changing the selected columns to student_id and name answers a different, equally legitimate question that the task would have to request.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT name
FROM students
WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND gpa >= 3.5
ORDER BY name;
```

ORDER BY gives the report a deterministic presentation under its stated comparison rules. Classical relations are unordered. LIMIT, top-N selection, or pagination introduces additional considerations beyond merely displaying the same relation in a chosen order. Do not move filters across row limits while assuming the membership remains unchanged.

## Logical equivalence needs stated conditions

Splitting an AND selection into successive selections over the same available attributes can preserve the intended relation. Pushing a student-only predicate below an inner join can also preserve matching results under the appropriate conditions. These are semantic observations, not a promise that every textually similar rewrite works across all SQL features.

Outer joins require particular care. A predicate applied after unmatched rows are padded can eliminate them, whereas placing that predicate in the matching condition can preserve left candidates. Volatile expressions, aggregates, row limits, and SQL duplicate semantics can introduce further differences. Before applying an algebraic identity to SQL, check the actual operator variant and result contract.

## Logical description differs from physical execution

The optimizer may choose a different join order, access path, or algorithm while preserving the query's defined result. Writing an inner join after a filter does not force a literal execution sequence through those textual clauses. Conversely, a compact expression is not automatically faster than a longer equivalent expression. Physical cost depends on data distribution, indexes, statistics and engine behaviour.

An algebra trace helps explain correctness; an execution plan helps inspect the chosen strategy. Neither alone proves production performance. A small fixture can reveal a wrong match or duplicate, but it cannot establish workload latency for large tables. Keep semantic tests, engine-specific plan inspection, and production performance measurements as separate forms of evidence.

## Validate composition with counterexamples

Use repeated names with different student identities, several enrollments per student, a student with no enrollment, and a closed course. Those cases expose whether the report returns names, students or enrollment occurrences. Add an unmatched proposal when the exercise schema permits it, so the effect of an inner match is visible rather than assumed from perfectly clean samples.

For predicates, test a GPA exactly at 3.5 and a nearby lower value. If GPA is nullable, an ordinary comparison to 3.5 is not TRUE for the missing value; the policy for unknown GPA must be explicit. The introductory fixture uses a required GPA field to keep its boundary simple. A different nullable model would need its own cases and explanation.

## Build a readable expression before considering rewrites

Start with a clear population, identify required relationships, apply the intended predicates, and retain the exact output roles. Trace at least one included and one excluded candidate. Then ask whether any intermediate step discards information or multiplies occurrences unexpectedly. This sequence turns a long expression into a chain of checkable contracts rather than a string of unfamiliar symbols.

Only after membership and grain are correct should equivalent formulations be compared for clarity or measured performance. Preserve the empty-input behaviour, duplicate handling and identifier scope while rewriting. The exercises focus on those observable result contracts; their reference fixtures do not prove that an arbitrary submitted query used a particular algebraic transformation or that a hosted provider chose the same execution plan.

questions.question_text: What does a composed relational algebra expression describe?
options: A single, atomic operation like Selection alone
A relational result formed by operators whose outputs can feed later operators
A special SQL keyword
A type of database index
questions.explanation: A simple base or operator expression is also valid; composition builds larger expressions through closure.

questions.question_text: In π(name)(σ(department = 'Engineering')(Students)), which operation is applied FIRST?
options: Projection (π), since it's written first
Selection (σ), since algebra notation nests inside-out like function calls
Both are applied simultaneously
Neither — this notation is invalid
questions.explanation: Just like nested function calls, the innermost operation (Selection here) executes first, feeding its result to the outer operation (Projection).

questions.question_text: Does the order operations are conceptually written in an algebra expression always match the order a real database engine executes them?
options: Yes, always, exactly
Not necessarily — a query optimizer can reorder operations (e.g. applying Selection before a Join) to improve performance while preserving the same correct result
Real engines always execute right-to-left, opposite to the written order
Execution order has no bearing on correctness or performance
questions.explanation: Query optimizers routinely reorder logically-equivalent operations for efficiency — this is covered further in Chapter 35.

questions.question_text: How would you build the expression for 'names of Engineering students with GPA >= 3.5'?
options: A single Projection alone is sufficient
Select the qualifying rows first, then project onto just the name column
Project first, then select
Use only a Join operation
questions.explanation: Filtering to the right rows (Selection) before narrowing to the desired column (Projection) is the natural composition here.

questions.question_text: Can the same real-world question be expressed by more than one equivalent relational algebra expression?
options: No, there is always exactly one correct expression
Yes — multiple equivalent expressions can answer the same question, and recognizing which is more efficient is a query-optimization skill
Only if the question involves exactly one table
Equivalent expressions always have identical performance
questions.explanation: Equivalent expressions preserve the defined result; performance still needs engine and workload evidence.

questions.question_text: What is a reliable strategy for constructing a complex relational algebra expression (or SQL query)?
options: Always write the entire expression in one attempt with no intermediate checks
Build it incrementally from the base relations, adding one operation at a time and checking each intermediate result
Only ever use a single operation, no matter how complex the question
Memorize a fixed template for every possible question
questions.explanation: Incremental construction with intermediate verification is a much more reliable method than attempting the full expression at once.

questions.question_text: How does a question needing data from three related tables typically get expressed?
options: It cannot be expressed in relational algebra at all
By chaining Joins between the tables (matching on shared keys), then applying Selection/Projection as needed on the combined result
By using only Projection three times
By using three separate, unrelated queries with no way to combine them
questions.explanation: Multi-table questions typically chain Joins to combine the data, then filter/narrow with Selection/Projection.

questions.question_text: Why does SQL's clause-based syntax feel more 'linear' than algebra's inside-out nested notation, despite expressing the same composition?
options: SQL doesn't actually compose multiple operations the way algebra does
SQL clauses (FROM/JOIN, WHERE, SELECT) are written in a fixed sequential order rather than as nested function-call-style notation, even though the underlying composition of operations is equivalent
Algebra and SQL are unrelated concepts with no correspondence
SQL only ever supports a single operation per query
questions.explanation: SQL clause syntax differs from nested notation; SQL bags, NULL and ordering need explicit treatment rather than blanket equivalence to classical set algebra.

questions.question_text: Which property allows one algebra result to become another operator’s input?
options: Permanent disk ordering
Closure over relations
Automatic foreign keys
Unique display names
questions.explanation: The intermediate result remains a relation with a defined heading.

questions.question_text: When does projecting only names lose information needed by a later GPA filter?
options: Only after ORDER BY
Never
When GPA is removed before that filter
Only if all names differ
questions.explanation: Later predicates require their referenced roles to remain available.

questions.question_text: Two qualifying students share a name. What does set projection onto name return?
options: Two student identities automatically
No values
One distinct name value
One arbitrary student record
questions.explanation: Projection grain differs from person identity.

questions.question_text: Which SQL feature mirrors duplicate-eliminating projection for selected name values?
options: SELECT name alone always
ORDER BY alone
An alias alone
SELECT DISTINCT name
questions.explanation: Ordinary SELECT is duplicate preserving.

questions.question_text: A student has three matching enrollments. What can a SQL inner join produce?
options: Three student-enrollment occurrences
Always one student row
Always no row
A uniqueness constraint automatically
questions.explanation: Multiplicity follows the matching facts.

questions.question_text: What must an early projection retain?
options: Only whichever label looks shortest
Attributes required by later predicates, joins and output
Only the final display name in every query
No identifiers
questions.explanation: Projection movement must preserve information needed downstream.

questions.question_text: Does an algebra trace prove the physical join algorithm?
options: Yes; nested notation forces nested loops
Only when DISTINCT appears
No
Only with three tables
questions.explanation: Logical meaning and physical execution are separate.

questions.question_text: Which movement is unsafe without further analysis?
options: Renaming a local table alias consistently
Keeping every required output role
Tracing a base relation
Moving a right-side filter across an outer join
questions.explanation: Unmatched row preservation can change.

questions.question_text: Which sample best reveals name-value versus student-identity grain?
options: Two different students with the same displayed name
One student with a unique name
Only empty courses
A different page title
questions.explanation: The two contracts produce visibly different cardinalities.

questions.question_text: Why include complete keys in a three-input expression?
options: To force one specific query plan
To match the intended scoped identities
To authorize every caller
To sort names automatically
questions.explanation: Local identifiers can collide across scopes.

questions.question_text: What does ORDER BY add to a set-style report?
options: A new foreign key
Automatic duplicate elimination
A presentation order under the selected comparison rules
A guarantee of one row per person
questions.explanation: Classical relation membership has no inherent display order.

questions.question_text: When should performance claims be made?
options: Whenever an expression has fewer symbols
After only a diagram
Whenever an alias is shorter
After relevant engine and workload evidence
questions.explanation: Correctness reasoning alone does not measure physical cost.

coding_problems.title: Select qualifying students and project distinct name values
coding_problems.task: Return distinct name values of Engineering students with gpa >= 3.5. This is a name-value set, not one row per student.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL, department VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, gpa DECIMAL(3,2) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.ordering: Ascending name. Fixtures use canonical labels without collation ambiguity.
constraints: Filter on department and GPA before projecting the name-value set.
edge_cases: Two qualifying students can share a name.
hints: Use DISTINCT for the requested name-value set.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT DISTINCT name FROM students WHERE department='Engineering' AND gpa>=3.5 ORDER BY name;
coding_problems.explanation: Selection chooses qualifying facts and duplicate-eliminating projection produces the requested name values.

coding_problems.title: Compose two associations into a distinct student report
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and name once per Engineering student with at least one enrollment in an open course (is_open=1). Multiple qualifying enrollments must not duplicate the student.
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha','Engineering'),(2,'Asha','Engineering'),(3,'Ben','Science'),(4,'Chen','Engineering'); INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,1),(20,1),(30,0); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,30),(3,10);
constraints: Return student identity, not distinct display-name values.
edge_cases: Several matching enrollments do not duplicate one student.
A closed course does not qualify a student.
An unmatched course proposal supplies no open course.
hints: Match enrollment to both its student and course.
Project the requested distinct student identity.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT DISTINCT s.student_id,s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id=s.student_id JOIN courses c ON c.course_id=e.course_id WHERE s.department='Engineering' AND c.is_open=1 ORDER BY s.student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The associations and selections produce qualifying participation facts, then distinct student identity sets the final grain.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha','Engineering'),(2,'Asha','Engineering'); INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,1); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10),(1,10),(2,10);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Asha','Engineering'); INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,99);
